slides: Let's continue with two letters, and two more cases.

slides.say: Two letters may get the same number, unless the question says they're different. Giving them the same number is often the fastest. For example, the bracket a plus three, times the bracket b plus three. From that product we subtract three a, three b, and a b. The choices are zero, three, six and nine.
There's no restriction, so let's take zero for both letters. Zero plus three is three, and three times three is nine. Three a, three b and a b are all zero. So the expression is nine.
The choices are numbers, so only one of them can be nine, choice number four. One try is enough.
With letters in the choices, the same number can make two choices tie. Look at two choices, a squared b, and a b squared. With a and b both one, both choices give one.
at: With a and b both one

slides.say: So we keep a as one, and we change b to two. Then we check only those two choices. a squared b is one times two, two. And a b squared is one times four, four. Now they're different. So different letters don't need different numbers. We change one only when the same number makes choices tie.
at: a squared b is one times two
And a b squared is one times four

slides.say: A third case. Sometimes there are no letters at all, but an amount is unknown, and they ask for a ratio or a part. In a ratio, the actual numbers don't matter. One to two, two to four and ten to twenty are the same ratio.
at: One to two, two to four

slides.say: So I may choose the amount myself. For example, half of a number plus a third of the same number. What part of the number is it?
at: half of a number plus a third

slides.say: Which number? Six, because both two and three go into it. Half of six is three, and a third of six is two. Together five, out of six. So it's five sixths of the number, whatever the number is.
The fourth case. An equation, but with more letters than equations, and they ask for one value. For example, four x plus six y equals eighteen. What is six x plus nine y?

slides: An equation with two letters can have many allowed solutions. Sometimes the result they ask for changes between them. Then it cannot be determined. But here, both terms they ask for are one and a half times the terms in the given equation. So their sum is fixed too. Let's use one easy solution to calculate it.

slides.say: I give one letter a value, and I solve the equation for the other. x equals zero, because multiplying by zero makes the whole x term zero. Then six y equals eighteen, so y is three.
at: I give one letter a value

slides.say: Now what they ask. Six times zero is zero, and nine times three is twenty-seven. So six x plus nine y is twenty-seven.

slides: Here zero makes the calculation easy, and it's allowed. But I chose only x. The equation then made y equal to three. I can't choose both letters freely: they still have to satisfy the equation.

slides.say: And it's really true. Six x plus nine y is one and a half times four x plus six y, because each part is one and a half times as big. And one and a half times eighteen is twenty-seven.

One more trick for choosing the number. In a story with letters, look for an allowed value where nothing changes. If nobody joins or nothing is added, sometimes we know the result without a formula. But that value must still be allowed by the question.

For example, n friends rent a boat for P shekels and share the cost. Then k more friends may join. In this example k may be zero: nobody has to join. They share the cost again. By how much less does each one pay?
Plug in k equals zero. Nobody joined, so nobody pays less, and the answer must be zero. So every choice that doesn't give zero when k is zero is out, with no calculation at all.
This value often leaves two choices. Then use a tie-breaker, an ordinary number like k equals one, and check only the two that are left. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
